title: Decision trees
blurb: An AI you can actually read. Learn how a tree of yes/no questions makes smart choices.

steps.title: The AI you can read
steps.body:
Some AIs are a mystery box — they give an answer but can't explain *why*.

A **decision tree** is the opposite. It makes choices with a chain of simple **yes/no questions**, exactly like a game of 20 Questions. You can read every step. Let's build one.

steps.title: It's just questions
steps.body:
Picture sorting fruit. You might ask: *"Is it sweet?"* If yes → probably an apple. If no → probably a lemon.

That single question is a **split**: it cuts your pile into two groups. String a few splits together and you've got a tree that can sort almost anything.

steps.title: Make your own split
steps.body:
Below are apples and lemons, plotted by **sweetness** and **size**.

Pick a measurement to split on, then drag the cut line. Watch the rule and the **accuracy** change. Try to find the split that sorts them best!

steps.title: Find the best split
steps.body: Choose 'sweetness' or 'size', then slide the cut. Aim for the highest accuracy.

steps.title: Notice anything?
steps.body:
Splitting on **sweetness** probably got you way higher accuracy than **size**. That's because sweetness *separates* apples from lemons much better — it's a more useful feature (remember features from lesson 2?).

A decision tree always hunts for the question that splits the data **cleanest**.

steps.title: Best question
steps.question: A decision tree is choosing its first question. Which one does it pick?
choices: The question that splits the groups most cleanly
The last question in the list
steps.explain: It picks the cleanest split — the question that best separates the groups. Cleaner splits = more accurate.

steps.title: One split isn't enough
steps.body:
Your single cut probably missed a few fruits. Real trees fix that by asking **another** question on each side.

*"Is it sweet?"* → if no, *"is it tiny?"* → … Each new question is a branch, and the tree gets deeper and smarter. That branching shape is exactly why it's called a *tree*.

steps.title: Growing the tree
steps.question: How does a decision tree become more accurate?
steps.explain: More good questions = more branches = a tree that separates the groups more finely.

steps.title: The superpower: you can explain it
steps.body:
Here's what makes trees special. If a tree says *"this is a lemon,"* it can show you exactly why: *"because it wasn't sweet, and it was small."*

That's called being **explainable** (a "white box"). Doctors, banks, and judges love trees for this — when an AI affects someone's life, being able to explain the *why* really matters.

steps.title: White box vs black box
steps.question: Why might a hospital prefer a decision tree over a mystery-box AI?
choices: You can see and explain exactly why it made each decision
steps.explain: Explainability! A tree can show its reasoning step by step — crucial when a decision affects a real person.

steps.title: The catch: don't overthink it
steps.body:
Remember **overfitting** from the regression lesson? Trees can do it too.

If a tree keeps adding questions until every single example is perfectly sorted, it just **memorized** the data and will flub new fruit. Good trees stay short enough to learn the real pattern, not the noise.

steps.title: Recap
steps.question: What's the main reason decision trees are so popular?
choices: They make explainable decisions from simple yes/no questions
steps.explain: Simple, explainable yes/no logic — that's the decision tree's whole appeal.

steps.title: What you learned 🎉
steps.body:
- A **decision tree** sorts things with a chain of **yes/no questions** (splits)
- It picks the question that splits the data **cleanest** (best feature)
- More branches = smarter, but too many = **overfitting**
- Its superpower is being **explainable** — it can always show its reasoning

**Next up:** the AI behind the headlines — **neural networks**. You'll teach a tiny digital 'brain' to learn.
